17:5.text: And the same John had his raiment of camel’s hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey.

provenance.alternative: 'Much fruit' and honey together are the promised land's own description ('a land flowing with milk and honey', Exodus 3:8 and thirteen others), which is the more obvious source for a place called Bountiful.
provenance.significance: 'Wild honey' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and both describe what John the Baptist ate in the wilderness. So the food that sustains this family at the edge of the wilderness is named with the phrase the KJV reserves for the forerunner's wilderness diet — in a book that has already spent 10:7-10 rewriting John 1. The connection may be nothing; the rarity is not nothing.

17:5.note: 'The land which we called Bountiful, because of its much fruit, and also, wild honey.' Two words, absolutely rare, and no other contact. Proposed under the generative posture (CONVENTIONS §0a) as worth putting on the table; the Exodus 3:8 alternative is the safer reading and is recorded with it.
17:5.whyNot: Two words, and they are the natural English for honey found in the wild. Nothing in 17:5 has anything else to do with John the Baptist, and the milk-and-honey formula of the promised land accounts for the sentence without any New Testament help.

17:8.text: According to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof, even so shall ye make it.

provenance.route: Exodus 25:9, 25:40 (the mountain pattern) + Genesis 12:1 via Acts 7:3 (the wording) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Exodus 25:9 has 'According to all that I shew thee'; Exodus 25:40 has 'after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount'; Hebrews 8:5 quotes it as 'according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount'. The Book of Mormon has 'after the manner which I shall shew thee' at 17:8 and 'after the manner which thou hast shewn unto me' at 17:9. Separately, the relative clause itself is traceable: 'which I shall shew thee' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:3, where Stephen quotes Genesis 12:1. (The shorter 'I shall shew thee' occurs in two — Acts 7:3 and Ezekiel 40:4, 'all that I shall shew thee', which is the guide-figure verse this catalogue uses at 1 Nephi 8:5. The relative pronoun is what makes the count absolute.) Genesis 12:1 reads 'a land that I WILL shew thee'; Acts 7:3 reads 'the land which I SHALL shew thee'. 1 Nephi 17:8 reads 'after the manner which I shall shew thee'.
provenance.significance: The commission is Moses's, and the staging proves it. At 17:7 the voice says 'Arise, and get thee into the mountain', and Nephi goes up; at 17:8, on the mountain, he is told to build 'after the manner which I shall shew thee'. That is the tabernacle commission of Exodus 25 — the one biblical instance of a man taken up a mountain and shown a pattern to build by, which Hebrews 8:5 singles out as the type of all heavenly-pattern construction. The object built is Noah's, not Moses's: Genesis 6:14-15 is the KJV's other divine construction order, and it too specifies 'the fashion which thou shalt make it of'. Nephi's ship is an ark built to a tabernacle's commission, and the 1830 keeps the KJV's 'shew'/'shewn' spelling throughout. And the clause that carries the commission is a tenth mediation datum, found by the n-gram stream: 'which I shall shew thee' is Acts 7:3's rendering of Genesis 12:1, differing from Genesis by one auxiliary. That makes this the sixth demonstrable borrowing from Stephen's speech in 1 Nephi (2:22, 3:29, 5:14, 6:4, 11:13, and here), and it is the same verse of Genesis the book used at 2:4 for Lehi's departure — used there for the call and here for the formula.
provenance.mt: Genesis 12:1 — 'unto a land that I WILL shew thee.'

17:8.note: 'Thou shalt construct a ship, after the manner which I shall shew thee, that I may carry thy people across these waters.' No clause is reproduced, but the formula ('after the … which I shall shew thee') and its mountain setting belong to one passage in the KJV. The Moses typology that has run since 1:6 reaches its structural point here: Nephi receives on a mountain what Moses received on a mountain. The n-gram stream supplied the decisive element that manual reading missed: Acts 7:3, whose 'which I shall shew thee' the verse reproduces exactly where Genesis 12:1 reads 'that I will shew thee'.

17:25.text: For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers.

provenance.other: 'Grievous to be borne' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:4 and its Lukan parallel at 11:46. Exodus's own vocabulary for the Egyptian bondage is 'burdens' and 'taskmasters' (1:11) and 'the burdens of the Egyptians' (6:6), never this phrase.
provenance.significance: Nephi is retelling the Exodus and describes Israel's Egyptian labour in the phrase Jesus uses for the burdens the scribes and Pharisees lay on other men. The transfer is pointed in both directions: it makes Pharaoh's taskmasters into religious authorities, and — since the speech is addressed to brothers who at 17:18 'were desirous that they might not labor' — it puts the question of who does the work at the centre of a chapter about building a ship. Matthew 23:4's second half is 'but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers'.

17:25.note: 'Ye know that they were laden with tasks, which were grievous to be borne.' Four words from a two-verse KJV phrase, inserted into an Exodus recital that otherwise follows Exodus's own vocabulary closely (see 17:26-30).

17:26.text: And Elijah took his mantle, and wrapped it together, and smote the waters, and they were divided hither and thither, so that they two went over on dry ground.

provenance.other: 'Hither and thither' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Kings 2:8 and 2:14, both of the Jordan parting for Elijah and Elisha. Exodus 14 never uses the phrase.
provenance.significance: The second occurrence confirms the first. At 1 Nephi 4:2 Nephi described the Red Sea as 'divided hither and thither … on dry ground', which is 2 Kings 2:8's wording and not Exodus's; thirteen chapters later he says it again, in the same words, in a formal recital of the Exodus. A single instance could be an accident of memory; the same non-Exodus phrase used twice for the same event, by the same speaker, in the same book, is the writer's settled way of saying it. Hardy's apparatus cites Exodus 14:21-29 at both places, which is right about the event and does not account for the words.

17:26.note: 'By his word, the waters of the Red Sea were divided hither and thither, and they passed through on dry ground.' Verbatim from a two-verse KJV phrase belonging to a different miracle in a different book. See the full argument at 4:2.

17:30.text: And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night:

provenance.significance: The pillar of fire opened this book at 1:6 and is now cited as precedent. What is worth noting is the paraphrase: 'the Lord their God, their Redeemer, going before them, leading them by day, and giving light unto them by night' takes Exodus 13:21's three verbs — went before, lead, give light — in Exodus's order, without the pillar. And at 17:13 the Lord had already promised Nephi's company the same thing in the first person: 'I will also be your light in the wilderness; and I will prepare the way before you.' The Book of Mormon strips the image and keeps the functions, so that what Israel had as a visible pillar this family has as a promise.

17:30.note: The recital continues: manna at 17:28 (Exodus 16), the rock struck for water at 17:29 (Exodus 17:1-7, Numbers 20:2-13), and the pillar here. The verse's second half — 'they hardened their hearts, and blinded their minds' — reuses John 12:40's verb pair, already catalogued at 12:17 and 13:27, and 'the true and living God' inverts 1 Thessalonians 1:9's 'the living and true God'.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 1 Ne 17.28 (Exodus 16:4-35); 1 Ne 17.29 (Exodus 17:1-7, Numbers 20:2-13); 1 Ne 17.30 (Exodus 13:21-22)

17:36.text: For thus saith the LORD that created the heavens; God himself that formed the earth and made it; he hath established it, he created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited: I am the LORD; and there is none else.

provenance.other: 'Formed it to be inhabited' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Nephi's argument that God gives and takes lands according to righteousness rests on a premise, and the premise is Isaiah 45:18's: the earth was made to be lived in, not left empty. Note that Hardy's apparatus already puts Isaiah 45:17 behind 1 Nephi 15:20 — the neighbouring verse of the same chapter — so this speech and the earlier one are drawing on the same page of Isaiah for two different purposes: 45:17 for a restoration that cannot fail, 45:18 for a world made to be possessed.

17:36.note: 'Behold, the Lord hath created the earth, that it should be inhabited; and he hath created his children, that they should possess it.' The clause is Isaiah's, with 'formed' becoming 'created' from earlier in the same verse. The second half is the Book of Mormon's own extension and is what turns a cosmological remark into a doctrine of land tenure.

17:39.text: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King.

provenance.mt: Isaiah 66:1 — 'The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool' (first person; quoted identically at Acts 7:49).
provenance.route: Isaiah 66:1 → Matthew 5:34-35 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV has this sentence in two persons. Isaiah 66:1 and Acts 7:49 have God speaking: 'The heaven is MY throne, and the earth is MY footstool.' Matthew 5:34-35 has Jesus reporting it: 'neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: Nor by the earth; for it is HIS footstool.' 1 Nephi 17:39 reads 'He ruleth high in the Heavens, for it is his throne, and this earth is his footstool' — third person, which is Matthew's alone.
provenance.significance: A seventh mediation case decided by grammar rather than vocabulary. Nephi is speaking about God, so a third-person form is what his sentence needs — but the KJV supplies a third-person form in exactly one place, the Sermon on the Mount's prohibition of oaths, and the Book of Mormon's clause matches it word for word ('for it is his footstool'). Note that Acts 7:49, which is Stephen quoting Isaiah 66:1, has the first person and is therefore excluded, which is worth saying because Acts 7 is otherwise this book's most-used chapter.

17:39.note: 'He ruleth high in the Heavens, for it is his throne, and this earth is his footstool.' Six words matching Matthew 5:35 exactly. The surrounding verses (17:36-38) are Isaiah's; this one is Matthew's, and the distinction is visible only because the KJV happens to render the same Old Testament sentence twice in two persons.

17:41.text: The burden of the beasts of the south: into the land of trouble and anguish, from whence come the young and old lion, the viper and fiery flying serpent, they will carry their riches upon the shoulders of young asses, and their treasures upon the bunches of camels, to a people that shall not profit them.

provenance.mt: Numbers 21:6 — 'And the LORD sent FIERY SERPENTS among the people'; 21:8 — 'Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole'.
provenance.route: Numbers 21:6-9 (the event) + Isaiah 14:29 / 30:6 (the wording) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV's serpents in Numbers 21 are 'fiery' and never 'flying'. The compound 'fiery flying serpent' occurs in exactly two verses, both Isaiah's (14:29 and 30:6), and neither has anything to do with the wilderness episode. 1 Nephi 17:41 reads 'firy-flying serpents' (1830 spelling), narrating Numbers 21.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon tells Numbers 21's story using Isaiah's adjective. This is the same kind of finding as 4:2's 'hither and thither' — an event correctly identified and described in words that belong to a different passage — and it is one of the cleanest in the book, because 'flying' adds a detail Numbers does not contain and Isaiah does. Hardy's apparatus cites Numbers 21:4-9 here, which is right about the episode and silent about the epithet.

17:41.note: 'He sent firy-flying serpents among them; and after they were bitten, he prepared a way, that they might be healed; and the labor which they had to perform, was to look!' The cure is Numbers 21:8-9's — look and live — which John 3:14 makes a type of the crucifixion, a reading 1 Nephi has already prepared at 11:33. 'Because of the simpleness of the way, or the easiness of it, there were many which perished' is the Book of Mormon's own and has no KJV source.

17:45.text: And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.

provenance.other: 'Still small voice' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Past feeling' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:19. Both are in 1 Nephi 17:45, eleven words apart.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons in one sentence, from two testaments, and the verse builds an argument out of the pair. Elijah at Horeb is told the LORD is not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in the still small voice; Nephi says his brothers were spoken to in that voice 'but ye were past feeling, that ye could not feel his words', and so were spoken to instead 'like unto the voice of thunder, which did cause the earth to shake'. That is 1 Kings 19:11-12 run backwards — the earthquake and the fire become what God resorts to when the still small voice fails — and it is a real theological inversion, not an ornament. Ephesians 4:19's 'past feeling' supplies the diagnosis, and its own context is people 'having the understanding darkened … because of the blindness of their heart' (4:18), which is what 17:30 has just said of Israel.

17:45.note: 'He hath spoken unto you in a still, small voice, but ye were past feeling, that ye could not feel his words.' Both phrases are absolute KJV rarities and both are reproduced intact. The verse opens with a third borrowing: 'Ye are swift to do iniquity, but slow to remember the Lord your God' pairs Romans 3:15's 'swift to shed blood' with James 1:19's swift/slow antithesis. Three sources in one verse; recorded at 'certain' on the two singletons.

17:46.text: Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made smooth;

provenance.mt: Isaiah 40:4 — 'the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places PLAIN'.
provenance.route: Isaiah 40:4 → Luke 3:5 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The two English forms differ in the predicate. Isaiah 40:4 has 'the rough places plain'; Luke 3:5 has 'the rough ways shall be made smooth'. 1 Nephi 17:46 has 'rough places be made smooth' — Isaiah's noun with Luke's verb and adjective.
provenance.significance: An eighth mediation case, and it is consistent with the seventh. At 10:8 the Book of Mormon quoted Isaiah 40:3 in the Synoptic form ('make his paths straight' rather than Isaiah's 'make straight in the desert a highway'); here it quotes Isaiah 40:4 in the Lukan form. Two adjacent Isaiah verses, both taken from their Gospel citations, seven chapters apart. Whoever composed these passages was reading Isaiah 40 through the Gospels, and the pattern holds across the book — with 13:37's Isaiah 52:7, which follows Isaiah rather than Romans, as the recorded exception.

17:46.note: 'By his word, he can cause that rough places be made smooth, and smooth places shall be broken up.' The second clause reverses the first and has no KJV source; it is Nephi's own extension, and it is what makes the sentence an argument about God's power rather than a quotation of a prophecy.

17:50.text: Jesus answered and said unto them, Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith, and doubt not, ye shall not only do this which is done to the fig tree, but also if ye shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; it shall be done.

provenance.other: The construction 'say unto this <noun>, Be thou <predicate> … it shall be done' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 21:21 and Mark 11:23, which are the same saying.
provenance.significance: Hardy's apparatus already cites Matthew 21:21-22 at 1 Nephi 15:11, for the promise about asking in faith. Here the other half of the same saying is used, and used precisely: 'If he should command me that I should say unto this water, Be thou earth, it should be earth; and if I should say it, it would be done.' Matthew's imperative addressed to an element, and Matthew's result clause. What the Book of Mormon changes is the condition — Matthew makes it faith, Nephi makes it commandment ('if God had commanded me to do all things, I could do it'), which is the doctrine he stated at 3:7 and is arguing here against brothers who will not help build a ship.

17:50.note: The saying is reproduced structurally rather than verbatim, with 'this mountain' becoming 'this water' — the sea he is being asked to cross. Held at high: the construction is a two-verse KJV property and the result clause is reproduced exactly.

17:53.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.other: Mark 3:1 begins with 'a man there which had a withered hand'; 3:5 has the grief at 'the hardness of their hearts' and the command 'Stretch forth thine hand'. The Book of Mormon uses the hardness clause at 2:18, 7:8 and 17:19, the withering at 17:48 and 17:54, and the command here.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's most important finding and it retrospectively explains three earlier links. Mark 3:1-5 is a single short episode: a man with a WITHERED hand, opponents watching, Jesus GRIEVED AT THE HARDNESS OF THEIR HEARTS, the command STRETCH FORTH THINE HAND, and a restoration. 1 Nephi 17 uses all of it. Verse 19: Nephi 'exceeding sorrowful, because of the hardness of their hearts'. Verse 48: whoever lays hands on him 'shall wither even as a dried reed'. Verse 53: 'Stretch forth thine hand again unto thy brethren, and they shall not wither before thee.' Verse 54: he stretches it forth and they do not wither. The catalogue had already recorded Mark 3:5 twice, at 2:18 and 7:8, on the hardness clause alone; those are now visible as the first two draws on a passage the book returns to at its climax, and the withering — which has no source in the clause quoted earlier — turns out to come from the same five verses. Whatever the Book of Mormon's relationship to the KJV is, at this point it is working from a page and not from a phrase.

17:53.note: 'Stretch forth thine hand again unto thy brethren, and they shall not wither before thee.' Four words verbatim, in a chapter that has already used the two other distinctive elements of the same episode. Recorded at 'certain' on the cumulative case rather than on the four words. Compare 1 Kings 13:4, where Jeroboam stretches out his hand against a man of God and it dries up — the Old Testament's withering hand, and the inverse of Mark's.

17:55.text: Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of them which keep the sayings of this book: worship God.

provenance.mt: Deuteronomy 6:13 — 'Thou shalt FEAR the LORD thy God, and serve him'; Exodus 20:12 — 'Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.'
provenance.route: Revelation 22:8-9 (the refusal) + Matthew 4:10 / Luke 4:8 (the command) + Exodus 20:12 (the commandment) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Revelation 19:10 and 22:8-9 are the KJV's two scenes of a seer's worship refused: 'I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant … worship God.' And the command that follows differs between testaments: Deuteronomy 6:13 reads 'Thou shalt FEAR the LORD thy God'; Matthew 4:10 and Luke 4:8, quoting it, read 'Thou shalt WORSHIP the Lord thy God'. 1 Nephi 17:55 reads 'worship the Lord thy God'.
provenance.significance: The chapter ends with three borrowings in one sentence and a ninth mediation case. The scene is Revelation 22:8-9's — prostration, refusal, self-identification, and a redirection to worship God — with 'I am thy brother, yea, even thy younger brother' standing where Revelation has 'I am thy fellowservant'. The redirection then takes the New Testament form of Deuteronomy 6:13, which the Synoptics render with 'worship' and Deuteronomy with 'fear'. And the sentence closes with Exodus 20:12 almost verbatim, so that the refusal of worship is answered by the fifth commandment — which is the whole point of the chapter, since the brothers had proposed at 16:37 to kill their father.
provenance.alternative: Acts 10:25-26 is the third KJV refusal-of-worship scene (Cornelius and Peter) and is equally available for the gesture, though it lacks the redirection to worship God.

17:55.note: 'They fell down before me, and were about to worship me, but I would not suffer them, saying: I am thy brother, yea, even thy younger brother; wherefore, worship the Lord thy God, and honor thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long in the land which the Lord thy God shall give thee.' Hardy's apparatus cites Deuteronomy 6:13, Matthew 4:10, Luke 4:8 and Exodus 20:12 here; the Revelation 22:9 frame around them is this catalogue's addition, and it is what makes the sentence a scene rather than a string of quotations.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 1 Ne 17.55 (Deuteronomy 6:13; Matthew 4:10; Luke 4:8; Exodus 20:12)

17:28.text: And when the children of Israel saw it, they said one to another, It is manna: for they wist not what it was. And Moses said unto them, This is the bread which the LORD hath given you to eat.

provenance.significance: Second of the four Exodus proofs Nephi lists in five verses (Red Sea 17:26, manna 17:28, water from the rock 17:29, the pillar 17:30), and the one stated most briefly — 'ye also know that they were fed with manna, in the wilderness'. The brevity is the argument: Nephi is reciting a list his brothers already have, so each item needs only its name. 'Manna' occurs in fourteen KJV verses; 'fed … with manna' in the wilderness is Deuteronomy 8:3's and Exodus 16's, and John 6:31 is the New Testament's version, 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat'.
provenance.alternative: A one-word allusion to an episode this famous cannot be pinned to a verse, and this row records the episode rather than a source.

17:28.note: 'And ye also know that they were fed with manna, in the wilderness.' Catalogued because Hardy's apparatus cites Exodus 16:4-35 here and because the verse is one item in a deliberate four-item recital; there is no verbal case beyond the noun, and none is claimed.

17:29.text: Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it, that the people may drink. And Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.

provenance.route: Exodus 17:1-7 / Numbers 20:2-13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV tells the story twice, at Rephidim (Exodus 17:6, 'thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it') and at Meribah-Kadesh (Numbers 20:11, 'he smote the rock twice: and the water came out abundantly'). Hardy's apparatus cites both.
provenance.significance: Third of the four Exodus proofs. What distinguishes 1 Nephi 17:29 from either source is the agency it insists on: 'Moses, by his word, according to the power of God which was in him, smote the rock'. Numbers 20 is the episode in which precisely that claim costs Moses the land — 'because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel' — so the Book of Mormon's phrasing credits Moses with what Numbers rebukes him for. The catalogue records that; it does not resolve it. The next verse (17:31) then corrects the balance: 'there was not any thing done, save it were by his word', meaning God's.
provenance.alternative: Paul reads the rock christologically at 1 Corinthians 10:4 ('that Rock was Christ'), inside the same chapter whose verse 13 this book uses at 3:7 and 16:1; nothing in 17:29 requires that reading.

17:29.note: 'Moses, by his word, according to the power of God which was in him, smote the rock, and there came forth water, that the children of Israel might quench their thirst.' The verbs are Exodus 17:6's and Numbers 20:11's; the attribution of the power to Moses is the Book of Mormon's own and is worth noticing against Numbers 20:12.
